title: ICYMI: TSMC profit jumps nearly 70% on AI demand, but margin outlook weighs on shares
body: The results (released Thursday afternoon, Taiwan time) reinforce the AI investment theme for Asian chip and hardware stocks, with TSMC's view that demand is outrunning capacity supportive for suppliers across the semiconductor supply chain. The share reaction shows how high expectations are, though: a beat alone is no longer enough, and investors are now trading margins and cash flow. Taiwan's equity benchmark, where TSMC carries a heavy weighting, is likely to take its lead from how the stock trades in Taipei. Higher planned capital spending is a positive read-through for equipment makers. --- Background: TSMC set for sixth straight record profit as AI demand lifts Q3 earnings --- TSMC delivered the AI boom in numbers and told investors it is not slowing, but with the beat priced in, the market chose to fret about margins and the bill for all those new fabs. Summary: Q3 net profit rose nearly 70% to about NT$763 billion, slightly above LSEG consensus Revenue of about $47 billion beat the top of TSMC's own guidance range The gross margin was about 66%, down from Q2 on the early 2nm ramp AI-heavy high-performance computing made up 68% of revenue, and 2nm reached 8% of wafer revenue Q4 guidance is about $52 billion to $54 billion in revenue, with 2026 growth now seen at around 44% 2026 capex was reaffirmed at $60 billion to $64 billion, and US-listed shares slipped after the results Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

title: Moody's cuts Nike outlook to negative, sees earnings falling into fiscal 2028
body: The outlook change is a modest negative for Nike's bonds and adds to pressure on the shares, though the affirmed A2 rating limits any immediate impact on borrowing costs. The extended timeline for falling revenue and earnings is the more market-relevant signal, because it challenges expectations of a near-term recovery. A negative outlook raises the risk of a future downgrade, which would matter more for credit investors if earnings fail to stabilise. Broader consumer discretionary names may also face scrutiny over how long restructuring costs weigh on profits. - Moody's has not downgraded Nike, but by pushing its recovery out to fiscal 2028 it has put a timer on how long the turnaround can drag before the rating follows. Summary: Moody's changed Nike's outlook to negative and affirmed its A2 rating The agency said the turnaround is taking longer than it previously expected It expects revenue and earnings to fall through the fiscal year ending May 2027 and into fiscal 2028 Nike's strategic actions are expected to pressure earnings over that period That pressure is expected to constrain Nike's credit metrics Moody's Ratings has revised its outlook on Nike to negative while affirming the sportswear group's A2 credit rating, citing a turnaround that is taking longer than the agency had previously expected. In a statement released on Thursday, Moody's said it expects Nike's revenue and earnings to decline through the fiscal year ending in May 2027 and into fiscal 2028.

title: New Zealand card spending falls for second month as food prices hold flat in September
body: The data adds to a mixed picture for the New Zealand dollar, with weak household spending offsetting the stronger manufacturing survey released earlier in the day. A second monthly fall in card spending points to soft domestic demand, which tends to argue against tighter policy, while flat food prices remove one source of upward pressure on inflation for the month. Fuel costs, which manufacturers flagged as a key concern, remain the bigger swing factor for household budgets, leaving oil prices important for the consumer outlook. --- Yesterday: RBNZ's Conway says October rate decision completely open, OCR more likely to rise --- New Zealand's factories are finding their stride, but its shoppers are still keeping their cards in their wallets, and flat food prices are only a modest consolation. Summary: Seasonally adjusted electronic card retail spending fell 0.4% in September, after a 0.9% drop in August Actual card spending rose 0.9% from a year earlier, up from 0.2% in August Card data covers about 68% of core retail sales Food prices were unchanged on the month, after a 0.3% rise in August, and up 2.4% on the year Food accounts for nearly 19% of the consumers price index The weak consumer data contrasts with a strong manufacturing PMI released the same day New Zealand electronic card retail spending fell for a second straight month in September, while food prices held steady, according to data from Statistics New Zealand on Friday.

title: Japan's Foreign Bond Outflows Ease Slightly, Hinting at Softer Overseas Selling
body: Japan's foreign bond purchases showed a marginal easing in net outflows, with the latest reading improving to -339.7 billion from a previous -345.7 billion, according to data updated on 15 October 2026. Although the indicator remains in negative territory, signaling that Japanese investors are still net sellers of foreign bonds, the slightly smaller outflow suggests a modest reduction in overseas bond liquidation. Market participants may interpret the data as an early sign that pressures driving Japanese investors to repatriate capital could be stabilizing, though the overall trend continues to point to capital flowing back toward domestic assets. With global interest rate dynamics and currency movements in focus for Japanese institutional investors, the shift from -345.7 billion to -339.7 billion will be watched closely in the coming weeks for clues on whether this moderation in foreign bond selling is temporary or the beginning of a more sustained adjustment in portfolio flows. title: South Korea Jobless Rate Falls to 2-Year Low
body: South Korea's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate edged down to 2.6% in September 2026 from 2.7% in August, its lowest level since September 2024. The economy added 113,000 jobs during the month, extending gains for a fourth consecutive month and lifting total employment to 29.27 million, up from 29.15 million a year earlier. Job growth was driven primarily by health and social welfare services, which added 247,000 positions, followed by transportation and storage (+91,000) and financial and insurance activities (+81,000). In contrast, employment declined in accommodation and food services (-135,000), agriculture, forestry and fishing (-170,000), and education services (-42,000). title: NZX 50 Poised for Second Straight Weekly Gain
body: The NZX 50 rose 24 points, or 0.2%, to 13,857 in Friday morning trade, extending its gains for a third consecutive session and reaching its highest level since September 22. The benchmark followed overnight strength on Wall Street as the recent tech selloff abated and Treasury yields pulled back. Sentiment was further supported by fresh data showing an acceleration in New Zealand manufacturing activity in August. However, the advance was partially limited by a three-month high in food inflation and a continued decline in electronic card spending in September. Healthcare, consumer discretionary, and consumer staples stocks were the primary drivers of the move, with notable gains from Fisher & Paykel (up 1.1%), South Port of New Zealand (1.1%), Infratil (1.0%), and EBOS Group (0.5%). On a weekly basis, the index is on track for a 0.8% increase, which would mark its second consecutive weekly rise. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: New Zealand Electronic Card Spending Falls 0.4% in September
body: Seasonally adjusted electronic card transactions in New Zealand fell 0.4% month-on-month in September 2026, easing from a 0.9% decline in August. The smaller overall drop reflected a rebound in spending on consumables (up 0.3% vs down 0.4% in August) and motor vehicles (up 0.6% vs down 0.3%), alongside a faster rise in fuel spending (up 2.9% vs 1.3%). These increases were more than offset by weaker outlays on hospitality (down 2.3% vs down 1.9% in August), durables (down 0.5% vs down 1.6%), and apparel (down 2.0%, unchanged from August). On an annual basis, total electronic card spending grew 0.9%, picking up from a 0.2% increase in August, which had marked the slowest pace of growth since December 2025. title: New Zealand Food Inflation at 3-Month High of 2.4%
body: Annual food inflation in New Zealand quickened to 2.4% in September 2026, up from 1.9% in August, when it had marked the smallest increase since December 2024. This was the fastest pace of food price growth since June. The main driver was grocery food, with inflation in this category rising to 3.0% from 1.7% in August, making it the largest contributor to the annual increase in food prices. Inflation for restaurant meals and ready-to-eat food edged down slightly to 3.1% from 3.2%, but remained the second-largest contributor to overall food inflation. Prices for meat, poultry, and fish rose 3.2%, compared with a 3.4% increase in August, while fruit and vegetable prices fell more sharply, declining 1.8% after a 1.6% drop in the previous month. title: New Zealand Electronic Card Retail Sales Accelerate to 0.9% in September YoY
body: New Zealand's electronic card retail sales growth picked up in September 2026, with the year-over-year rate rising to 0.9%, up from 0.2% in August 2026. The latest figures, updated on 15 October 2026, point to a modest strengthening in consumer spending activity as captured through electronic transactions. The data compare the change in September's electronic card retail sales with the same month a year earlier, while the previous indicator reflected August's performance against August of the prior year. The move from 0.2% to 0.9% suggests that spending momentum via electronic payment methods has improved, albeit from a relatively subdued pace. While the overall level of growth remains moderate, the acceleration may be watched closely by analysts and market participants as a potential early sign of firmer retail demand heading into the final quarter of 2026. title: New Zealand Manufacturing Strengthens in September
body: New Zealand's BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index climbed to 56.5 in September 2026 from 53.2 in August, indicating a stronger expansion in manufacturing activity. Employment remained the softest sub-index at 51.8, but it stayed in expansionary territory and improved from 50 in August. The strongest gains came from Finished Stocks (59) and Deliveries (58.8), while both Production and New Orders advanced to 57. Despite the more robust headline result, sentiment was still mixed, with 53% of respondents' comments classified as negative. Participants continued to highlight elevated fuel costs and uncertainty in the lead-up to the election. However, some reported support from seasonal patterns, pre-Christmas ordering, and gradually improving demand. Overall, the solid readings in New Orders, Production, and Finished Stocks indicate that manufacturing momentum is building as the economy enters the final quarter of the year.
